title: Can interactive systems (human + machine) solve undecidable problems

problemStatement.formal:
orall A \subseteq \mathbb{N},\; A'

subseteq \Sigma^0_n\;\wedge\; orall f \colon \mathbb{N} 	o \mathrm{Bool},\; ( orall n,\, f\,n = [n \in K]) \Rightarrow  orall n,\,

problemStatement.plain: The prose question 'can interactive systems (human + machine) solve undecidable problems?' is decomposed into three concrete formal sub-goals on top of Mathlib's existing computability stack. OQ-03a: the Turing jump A' is never in Comp(A), so any 'machine + oracle A' system has its own halting problem strictly above A. OQ-03b: the arithmetical hierarchy is strict at every level, so no finite amount of oracle access decides all undecidable problems. OQ-03c: the classical halting set K is not Turing-reducible from any arithmetical oracle, so any 'interactive' hypercomputation that decides K must reach outside the arithmetical hierarchy. The OQ does NOT claim the Church-Turing thesis or refute Penrose-Lucas arguments about cognition.
whyMatters: Closes a long-standing prose gap in the halting-problem entry: the parent proof's openQuestions[2] is one of the most-cited 'soft' questions in the gallery, but never had a formal recursion-theoretic restatement.

Mathlib v4.26.0 has Computability.{Partrec, PartrecCode, Halting, TuringMachine} but no oracle TMs, no Turing jump, and no arithmetical hierarchy. OQ-03 motivates ~150-line oracle-TM API for the gallery and ~400-line arithmetical-hierarchy development as future side projects.

The diagonal argument in the parent's HaltingProblem.lean (172 lines, zero imports, zero axioms) lifts directly to the relativized case. OQ-03a is therefore the natural drop-in next step for the entry, requiring only oracle-parameterized Code.evaln.

Separates the recursion-theoretic content of the question (sub-goals OQ-03a/b/c, all formalizable) from the Church-Turing / philosophy-of-mind content (out of scope, explicitly so). This sharpens both halves of the literature.

open: OQ-03a: For every oracle A subset N, the relativized halting set A' = {e : M_e^A halts on e} is not in Comp(A). (Post 1944; classical.)
OQ-03b: For every n >= 0, Sigma^0_{n+1} is not contained in Sigma^0_n in the arithmetical hierarchy. (Mostowski 1947; equivalently Post's theorem 1948.)
OQ-03c: For the classical halting set K, no f : N -> Bool with f n = [n in K] is computable in any arithmetical oracle (any oracle in some Sigma^0_n). (Folklore consequence of OQ-03b.)

insights: The parent's HaltingProblem.lean diagonal argument (172 lines, zero imports, zero axioms) lifts verbatim to the relativized case: replace H : N -> N -> Bool with H^A and the diagonal D n = not (H n n) with D^A n = not (H^A n n). The contradiction H^A(D^A, D^A) = not H^A(D^A, D^A) is unaffected by the oracle. The only new content needed is a definition of Computable_in A.

Mathlib v4.26.0's Nat.Partrec.Code (in Computability.PartrecCode) is the right substrate: parameterize Code.evaln over an oracle by adding a Code.oracle constant (or by indexing the existing definition over o : N -> Bool). The S-m-n theorem (Nat.Partrec.Code.smn) and the fixed-point theorem (in Computability.Halting) are already mechanized and lift to the oracle setting.

Mathlib v4.26.0 has NO oracle TM and NO arithmetical hierarchy. The arithmetical hierarchy is a ~400-line side project (definitions of Sigma^0_n / Pi^0_n / Delta^0_n via quantifier prefix on partial recursive predicates + strictness proofs). OQ-03b is best deferred to its own multi-session arc.

Hypercomputation models (Zeno, ITTM, BSS, quantum) all reach outside the arithmetical hierarchy when they decide K, never within it: this is the formal content of OQ-03c. Quantum TMs are a popular misconception case: they decide exactly the same sets as classical TMs (BQP subset PSPACE subset R), so they are explicitly OUT of the hypercomputation discussion.

Church-Turing thesis is explicitly NOT a Lean theorem, and Mathlib's omission is correct. Each OQ-03 sub-goal is parameterized by an explicit oracle or model; CTT is mentioned only in the prose discussion sections, not in any theorem statement.

Penrose-Lucas claims about human cognition are out of scope for Lean formalization. They conflate consistency of a specific formal system with a description of cognition (Franzen 2005). OQ-03 produces machine-side theorems (no finite-level oracle decides K); cognition-side claims are left to the proof entry's prose.
mathlibGaps: No oracle Turing machines in Mathlib v4.26.0. The Computability.TuringMachine file defines TM0/TM1/TM2 but no oracle variant. OQ-03a's S2 deliverable is the first oracle TM (or oracle Code) in the gallery.
No Turing jump A' = {e : M_e^A halts on e} in Mathlib v4.26.0. The classical halting set K = jump emptyset is in HaltingProblem.lean indirectly (as no_halting_oracle) but not exposed as a Set.

No arithmetical hierarchy Sigma^0_n / Pi^0_n / Delta^0_n in Mathlib v4.26.0. Mathlib has descriptive set-theoretic hierarchies (Polish spaces, Borel sets) but no Kleene-style first-order hierarchy. ~400 lines to develop from scratch.
No Post's theorem (S in Sigma^0_n iff S is r.e. in jump^{n-1} of emptyset). The link between syntactic complexity and degree of unsolvability is missing.

No Rice's theorem in Lean 4 Mathlib (despite a stub in Computability.Halting; verify in S2 ACT-A). The parent's HaltingProblem.lean comment claims Rice is provable via Nat.rice but the full theorem may not be in v4.26.0.
